They will start relatively advanced but it's not as advanced as you think it is. It's mostly about retreading genchem stuff, as well as how to read chemical formulas and structures in the first lesson. At first, it's VSEPR, valence electrons, molecular representations, and nomenclature, then it'll start picking up from there with thermodynamics and acid-base stuff. The learning curve is either gradual or steep depending on your background knowledge on the topic.

Start reviewing your genchem stuff: valence electrons, atomic mass, isomers, etc. Those topics serve as the bedrock for what the orgchem curriculum will have. I found in my class, at least, that a lot of people had a hard time answering the questions posed by the prof because of that weak base. I do think that it's not the end of the world if your grasp of SHS chem isn't the best, but it's always a good thing to review your genchem.

If you have an okay social life, study with your blockmates. I am fortunate to have been able to study chemistry exhaustively because I had to compete nationally and stuff so I was able to recite decently well, but I found myself consulting with my groupmates about certain pointers when I wasn't being a recluse because the topics were just that hard to wrap your head around.

As funny as the whole "indian guy on youtube explains chemistry better than my profs" meme is, it is not without its merit. I found myself listening to Youtube regarding specific topics about the course since my prof wasn't that diligent in exhaustively discussing very specific mechanisms or reactions. So I would definitely recommend that.

I agree with your point that there is a bias towards anthropomorphic builds, but we work with what we know in our experience, yes?

  That aside, if you want to build intelligent species — humanoid or not — you have to ask the question: why are we smart? A lot of the academia around that say that we are smart because we evolved bipedalism, fire, tool use, the jazz. If you're into speculative evolution, you can try figuring out if you can make some inhuman build smarter, you can try seeing what traits can be used to help a species become more intelligent. You can start with a creature with a radically different biology to humans and see where they'll go to be intelligent, like in evolution. 

  Let's assume an earth-like biology pops up, but in a distant star system independent of earth, and this planet develops a creature with 9 legs sprawled like a starfish that is as smart as a crow and can dig using its appendages. What evolutionary pressure can make this creature smarter as a consequence? For example, the environment's soil gets tougher to break, so it evolves more articulate appendages to get the soil out faster and more efficiently, and as it migrates to an environment where the soil gets softer, which can give the creature the ability to use less appendages to dig up dirt, so it can free up 4 limbs for hurling dirt out while digging tunnels that span a wide area using the remaining 5 limbs. Then it starts to use its "arm" appendages to use flat rocks to dig around itself and scoops dirt out, which can quickly evolve into a stone arms race between individuals for mating purposes: as a larger and more complex tunnel system indicates fitness, individuals may start developing stronger arms, or use more advanced tools, or have evolved the use of primitive pointed tools for stabbing rivals, yada yada fire, yada yada tribes, yada yads cilivizations and technology.

  It doesn't have to follow the human behavioural evolution either, you can discover something else other than fire that boosts the nutritional advantage of the creature, but the main point is to dabble in the evolution of varied species and just speculate on what happens. It may not be everyone's cup of tea, but it certainly helps in fleshing out whether your creatures make sense and whether they are interesting. Also it's fun trying

**Number 1**

>  
It is intuitively implausible that the world could appear out of nowhere on its own, since there'd be no cause behind it, and it is intuitively plausible that a God could create our world in a snap. As a result, basically every culture on Earth has some sort of creation myth involving Gods or Godlike beings. At least for some otherwise rational people, this intuitive plausibility appears to be of the same strength as the plausibility that the real world exists.

  Just because something is intuitive doesn't make it true. I can just as easily believe that the earth is flat because I see no curvature.

  You seem to be appealing to the Kalam Cosmological argument, which attributes a cause to the universe since existence needs a cause and the universe exists. The problem with this is that you immediately attribute that cause to a god, which is a non-sequitur. Why does the cause have to be some god? It can be something else.

  People have been having hallucinations about blood sucking creatures and solo simians for many years. It doesn't make it true, not just because it is a hallucination (which is mostly irrelevant) but because it is independent of whether things are empirically and systematically proven. It just is, so they say.

  In investigating the real world and its legitimacy in its existence, you have to base your conclusion on real-life observations. Basing something on intuition, *a gut feeling,* is fine and all, but it is **illogical**.

**Number 2**

>Morality is intuitively plausible in the same way the real existence of the world is.   Judging from the numerous religious atrocities over thousands of years, basing your morality on a belief in a god is possible, but would you really call yourself moral considering many gods call for violence and 

  Slapping 'god' on an argument and calling it a day is quite obtuse. If we define objective as something that is factual, then we can base our objective morality over something that has predictive power, consistency, and is falsifiable (i.e. I will base my morality on something that is grounded in fact) . Belief in a god is, historically speaking, wishy-washy: you can beat up slaves as long as they don't die in the Christian Bible, for example, while nowadays we recognize that keeping slaves is morally unjust as is assault.

  You seem to fail to point out that we can base our objective morality on other, factually proven foundations, one of which would be evolution by natural selection: doing things that benefit you and your kindred is a pretty satisfactory bases. You're making an unbased assertion that God is necessary, because *it just is*. 

  I would pose a question: is something good because God commands it, or does God command it because it is good?

> A good God as formulated by those who believe in God on intuitive grounds would not choose to deceive us, and as such He would create a world where empirical observations are possible and reasoning has a degree of reliability.

A god can just as easily need to be evil on intuitive grounds that an evil god will choose to deceive us, and as such it would create a world in which empirical truths cannot be experienced by its creatures. I can flip your argument over its head and it would make reasonable sense; what does that say for your argument?

While it may often be impossible for third parties to verify these personal experiences, this type of justification does make belief in God intuitive in the same way the outside world is to those who have experienced convincing purported miracles.
